patterns.title: Names for the document
patterns.guidance: Each writer settles on a small set of names for the document and repeats them. Short writes this dissertation (31 times in the chapters) and this work (55), and also this dissertation work for what was done during the degree. Vázquez writes this dissertation (21) and this work (26). Bobu uses this dissertation and this thesis as equivalents (5 and 7). None of them calls the document a paper.
forms: This dissertation presents [contribution].
In this work, [term] is defined as [definition].
The remainder of this document is organized as follows.
[Analysis or dataset] was [performed / collected] as part of this dissertation work.
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Keep this dissertation for the whole program and this chapter for one study, as Hang's reference already says. This work is common in all three and is acceptable for a short reference to the program. Choose dissertation or thesis and use only that one. A chapter that came from a paper should not call itself this paper.

patterns.title: Verbs for what a chapter does
patterns.guidance: A chapter or the dissertation is the subject of a small set of verbs. Short uses presents, introduces, describes, reviews, and discusses. Vázquez uses presents, describes, and reviews. Bobu, who writes with we, uses propose, present, introduce, formalize, and showcase. The verb says what kind of content follows, so reviews announces literature, introduces announces a new model or method, and presents announces a study or its results.
forms: This chapter reviews [literature] in [fields].
This chapter introduces [model or method], in which [one-clause description].
This chapter presents [number] studies that [purpose].
This chapter describes [system or procedure].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: These verbs match the ones in Hang's reference. A chapter can present, introduce, review, or describe. It does not collect data or find results. Formalize promises a formal definition, so use it only where one follows.

patterns.title: Develop, instantiate, validate, evaluate
patterns.guidance: Short moves each contribution through a fixed chain of verbs. A model is formalized, an algorithm is developed from it, the algorithm is instantiated for one task, and the instance is validated or evaluated in a study. The same verbs return in every chapter opening and summary, so the reader always knows which step a sentence reports. Vázquez uses designed and built for the platform, evaluated for a method on a benchmark, and validated for an idea that an experiment tests. Bobu uses test for hypotheses and showcase for a demonstration of a framework in one setting.
forms: [Method] is instantiated for [task type] and evaluated in [study].
[Idea] was validated in [setting] with [participants].
[Framework] was evaluated on [benchmark or task] against [baselines].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Useful for the method chapters, where a general idea is followed by one implementation and one evaluation. Keep Hang's limit on validate, which needs a stated check. Evaluate does not say that the outcome was favorable.

patterns.title: Enable and leverage
patterns.guidance: Enable is the shared verb for what the research makes possible for a robot or a person. It appears 1.2, 0.9, and 1.4 times per 1,000 words in Short, Vázquez, and Bobu. Its object is an agent and an action, as in enable robots to detect. Leverage is rarer (0.2, 0.4, and 0.4 per 1,000 words) and means using something that already exists, such as a prior result, a dependency between two problems, or a dataset.
forms: [Method] enables [agent] to [action] without [requirement].
This chapter leverages [existing result or structure] to [purpose].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Both verbs are familiar to these readers, and leveraging is already in the title of the dissertation. Give enable an agent and an action. Hang's reference prefers the operation to a vague benefit, so follow enable with what the method does.

patterns.title: Insight, intuition, and observation
patterns.guidance: The central idea of a method is named as an idea before it is implemented. Vázquez writes our main insight is that and our key methodological insight. Bobu writes the core insight of this dissertation, the intuition is that, and our observation is that. Short uses insight for what a study yields, as in provides key insight into. The sentence that follows the label is short enough to remember and is repeated in the abstract, the chapter, and the conclusion.
forms: The main insight of this chapter is that [relationship].
The intuition is that if [condition], then [consequence].
[Study] provides insight into [question].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: This is the handoff from a finding to a method in Hang's reference. State the intuition once in a sentence and reuse that sentence. In the impersonal voice, the insight belongs to the chapter or the method.

A study finding leading to a method

patterns.title: Words for imperfect human input
patterns.guidance: Bobu's dissertation is the closest of the three to Hang's topic. Input from non-experts is called noisy, and features learned from it are called noisy or imperfect. The loss relative to experts is called degradation in input quality or degradation in performance. The claim that follows is measured against two reference points, an expert and a random baseline. Noisy input is described as input that still carries signal.
forms: [Non-expert input] was closer to [expert level] than to [random baseline] on [measure].
When given imperfect [inputs], [method] still [outcome] relative to [baseline].
With very noisy [inputs], the results are less conclusive.
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Hang's reference uses imperfections as the umbrella term and asks that noisy, sub-optimal, and unsuccessful each keep an operational definition. Bobu's wording supports the same stance, which is that imperfect teaching still contains information. The two reference points, expert and random, are a form worth reusing where the data allow it.

patterns.title: Graded words for evidence
patterns.guidance: The strength of a finding is graded in words that sit next to the number. Short writes some support, limited evidence, modest evidence, preliminary evidence, marginal significance, and a trend towards. Vázquez writes some evidence of and a trend suggested. Bobu writes provide evidence that, less conclusive, and less clear results. Strong words such as demonstrate and show are kept for results with a significant test or a clear margin.
forms: [Analysis] provides preliminary evidence for [pattern].
There was limited evidence that [outcome] (H[n]).
[Result] showed a trend towards [direction] ([statistic]).
The results are less conclusive when [condition].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: This agrees with Hang's rule that claim strength follows the evidence. Put the value next to the graded word, as Hang's reference asks for correlations. Marginal significance and trend need the p value beside them.

patterns.title: Suggest, may, might, could
patterns.guidance: Interpretations are hedged with a small set of words, and each writer has favorites. Suggest and its forms appear 1.2, 1.3, and 0.7 times per 1,000 words in Short, Vázquez, and Bobu. May appears 0.8, 0.9, and 1.9 times, might 1.0, 0.2, and 1.0 times, and could 0.7, 1.9, and 1.2 times. Short prefers might and suggesting that. Vázquez prefers could and tend to. Bobu prefers may. Hang's draft has 1.2 for suggest, 1.1 for may, 0.3 for might, and 1.2 for could, which is inside the range of the three.
forms: [Result], suggesting that [bounded interpretation].
This finding might indicate [interpretation].
[Group] tended to [behavior] when [condition].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Hang's reference gives each modal its own job, and the three dissertations use them the same way. No change in the amount of hedging is needed to match these readers. Keep the rule from the Chapter 8 review that can is not lowered to may as a matter of routine.

patterns.title: Prior work and efforts
patterns.guidance: Prior work is the usual phrase in Short and Vázquez, and Bobu titles a section Prior Work in most chapters. Vázquez also writes prior efforts and calls her own research our efforts. Bobu names method families by their standing, such as traditional methods, typical methods, and state-of-the-art methods. A sentence about prior work says what the work focused on or assumed, so that the next sentence can state what it leaves open.
forms: Prior work in [area] has primarily focused on [scope].
Traditional [methods] rely on [assumption or representation].
This chapter builds upon prior work on [topic].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Same phrase and same move as Hang's reference. Claims such as few studies and first still need literature support. Refer to Hang's own earlier studies by chapter.

patterns.title: Evaluative and emphatic words
patterns.guidance: The three differ most in how much evaluation their words carry. Short is restrained and uses novel, key, and particular promise in a few places. Vázquez uses essential and important for motivation and opens 7 sentences with Interestingly. Bobu is the most vivid, with notoriously challenging, vastly more complex, sorely needed, compelling evidence, and 15 sentences that open with Unfortunately. In the passages read, the strong word is usually attached to a problem or a need, and less often to the writer's own result.
forms: [Capability] is essential for [agents] to [goal].
[Approach] has particular promise for [application].
Selecting [object] is challenging, even for [experts], since [reason].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Hang's reference asks for value words used sparingly and next to the result that supports them. Short's restraint is the closest model. Bobu's stronger words are a personal register, and Hang's preference takes priority over it.

patterns.title: First person and the impersonal voice
patterns.guidance: This is the largest measured difference among the three, and between them and Hang's draft. We, our, and us appear 6.7 times per 1,000 words in Short, 18.0 in Vázquez, and 25.7 in Bobu. Hang's draft has 0.0. Short's abstract, introduction, chapter abstracts, and summaries are almost entirely impersonal, with this work, the model, and passive verbs as subjects, and we appears inside the study sections. Vázquez and Bobu use we throughout, also for work by the single author. Bobu changes to I in the final chapter for her own plans. Vázquez writes the author where she separates her part from a team's.
forms: [Topic] is formalized as [problem] in which [description].
This work presents [approach] that includes [parts].
[Algorithm] is validated in [study], and it is shown that [result].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Hang's dissertation is impersonal by default and that decision stands. Short's dissertation shows the same voice in the framing parts, so the adviser's own writing supports it. Since all three use we in study sections, a remaining we in a procedure would not look unusual to these readers. It is still replaced under Hang's own rule.

patterns.title: A result with its test
patterns.guidance: A quantitative result is one sentence that names the measure, gives the two values with their spread in parentheses, and gives the test with its statistic and p value. Short gives M and SD, the test, and often an effect size. Vázquez gives the test in parentheses after the factor name and M and SE for each condition. Bobu names the test and its factors in words and gives F and p. The verb is plain, such as showed, revealed, was significant, or found.
forms: Participants had higher [measure] in [condition A] (M = [a], SD = [b]) than in [condition B] (M = [c], SD = [d]).
A [test] on [measure] showed [result] (p = [value]).
[Factor] was significant ([statistic], p = [value]).
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Same content as Hang's reference, which asks for the measure, baseline, condition, and uncertainty together. Hang's reference uses compared with in a sentence and against inside parentheses. Do not add a test or a spread that the chapter did not compute.

patterns.title: A difference that was not found
patterns.guidance: A null result is reported as something the analysis did not find, and the sentence does not claim that the conditions are equal. patterns.guidance: Hypotheses are numbered and stated before the results. patterns.title: Possible explanations
patterns.guidance: An unexpected or weak result is followed by one or two candidate reasons, each marked as a possibility. Short writes this may have been because and may have been due to the fact that, and likely due to for the reason she finds most plausible. [Result] could be attributed to [reason]. An alternative explanation is that [reason].

patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Same as Hang's reference, which presents reasons as hypotheses that could be examined. Bobu's it is unclear whether is a useful form when two explanations remain open.

patterns.title: Limitations stated plainly
patterns.guidance: A limitation is announced in a short sentence and then listed with its consequence. Vázquez opens a discussion with the experiment was limited in several ways and counts the limits with First, Second, and Third. Short names the sample size, the interaction time, and the measure used as a proxy. Bobu states who the participants were and cautions that the result speaks to that population. The limit is tied to the design, and the writer does not apologize for it.
forms: The [study] was limited in several ways. First, [limit]. Second, [limit].
All [participants] had [property], so the results speak to [this population] and not to [the general population].
This study has a small number of participants and [other constraint].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Same as Hang's reference, where a limitation names the design constraint and the claim it limits. Bobu's caution about a technical sample is a model for the studies with recruited non-experts and crowdworkers.

patterns.title: Wording for future work
patterns.guidance: Future work is written with a modal that shows how firm the plan is. Short uses might, would, and could, and further research is needed to determine whether for an open question. Vázquez uses it would be interesting to explore and should. Bobu uses must for a gap in her own method, could for an option, and I plan to in the final chapter for work she intends to do. A direction is stated together with what it would make possible.
forms: Further research is needed to determine whether [question].
Future work could [action], which would [benefit].
One possible direction for future work is [topic]. Another area of future work is [topic].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Hang's reference uses Future work could and One planned step is to, with would for what a planned study does. Bobu's I plan to shows that planned work stated as a plan is accepted in a final chapter, and in Hang's impersonal voice this is one planned step. Write only what Hang's notes say.

A [type of contribution] of [object] wherein [what it does].

patterns.guidance: A term is defined in its own sentence when it first matters. forms: [Term] is defined in this work as [definition].
A [term] is a [category] that [distinguishing property].

patterns.title: Scope statements
patterns.guidance: Each writer says what the dissertation does not cover, early and in one or two sentences. Vázquez writes we limit the scope of this dissertation to and is out of the scope of this dissertation. Short writes is not directly addressed in this work and separates her topic from a neighboring one. Bobu states where a method was shown and where else it could apply. The excluded topic often returns as future work.
forms: The scope of this dissertation is limited to [setting or population].
[Topic] is not directly addressed in this dissertation.
[Term A] is distinguished from [term B], since [the model] applies only to [condition].
Although evaluated in [domain], [method] can be used in [other settings] where [condition].
patterns.in_hangs_dissertation: Hang's reference has no separate pattern for scope, so this one adds to it. A scope sentence in the Introduction answers a question that a committee member would otherwise ask at the defense.
